title: Nasdaq Futures Slip as Anthropic Misses Market Sentiment Boost – Live Updates】
body:
Wall Street opened Friday on a sour note, with Nasdaq‑100 futures sliding more than 2 % after the highly anticipated debut of AI start‑up Anthropic on the public markets failed to ignite investor enthusiasm. The broader market followed suit, as the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average each slipped over 2 % in early trading, extending a bleak session that saw technology‑heavy indexes tumble in the previous day’s close.

Anthropic’s initial public offering, which raised roughly $4 billion and valued the company at about $20 billion, was billed as a watershed moment for the next generation of generative‑AI firms. Yet the stock’s opening price hovered near its IPO price, and the modest first‑day performance did little to lift the broader AI rally that had buoyed the Nasdaq throughout the spring. Traders pointed to the company’s relatively modest product roadmap and a valuation that, while lofty, still lagged behind the sky‑high multiples enjoyed by peers such as OpenAI‑backed entities and the likes of Nvidia. The lack of a “pop” in Anthropic’s shares signaled that investors remain cautious about the sustainability of AI‑driven hype.

The tepid response to Anthropic reverberated across the technology sector, where several AI‑related stocks have been on a steep ascent over the past months. Nvidia, the chipmaker that has become synonymous with AI acceleration, saw its shares dip marginally as the broader sentiment cooled. Meanwhile, smaller AI specialists that had recently gone public—such as Stability AI and Cohere—experienced sharper declines, underscoring a market recalibration. Analysts suggest that investors are now demanding clearer paths to profitability and more concrete evidence that AI innovations can translate into recurring revenue streams, rather than relying on speculative growth narratives.

Beyond the AI theme, the market’s slide reflects a confluence of macro‑economic pressures that have been weighing on equities. Inflation data released earlier in the week showed persistent price pressures, keeping the Federal Reserve’s hawkish stance firmly in view. Bond yields have risen, pushing up borrowing costs for both consumers and corporations. In addition, the ongoing geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe and the Middle East have added a layer of uncertainty, prompting risk‑averse investors to retreat from growth‑oriented assets. The combination of these factors has amplified the impact of any disappointment in headline‑making IPOs, turning a single lackluster debut into a catalyst for broader market weakness.

Despite the current dip, some market participants remain optimistic about the longer‑term trajectory of AI investments. Venture capital flows into AI start‑ups continue to surge, and corporate spending on AI tools and infrastructure is still expanding at a rapid pace. Moreover, the sector’s talent pool is deepening, with leading research labs and universities churning out breakthroughs that could underpin the next wave of commercial applications. For investors, the key will be discerning which companies can move beyond experimental prototypes to deliver scalable, revenue‑generating products.

Looking ahead, the market’s direction will hinge on a handful of upcoming events. The Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting, slated for early next month, will be closely watched for any signals of rate adjustments. In the tech arena, the earnings reports of major AI‑enablers such as Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft are expected in the coming weeks and could either reaffirm the sector’s growth narrative or deepen the current pullback. Meanwhile, the performance of Anthropic in its first few weeks of trading will serve as a barometer for investor appetite for AI IPOs. If the company can demonstrate accelerating user adoption and a clear path to profitability, it may help restore confidence in the broader AI trade. Until then, traders are likely to proceed with caution, balancing the promise of artificial‑intelligence breakthroughs against the prevailing macro‑economic headwinds.
